blocks.text: Turkmens are known for their hospitality, and a visit to a Turkmen home follows customs that are easy to learn. Travel writers quote sayings that put the guest close to sacred, among them **a guest comes, happiness comes**, and note that people are often judged by how they treat their guests. According to one description of Turkmen customs, a traveller who reached a village was offered food and shelter in the first tent he came to, and could not leave without a warm meal.

**At the door, shoes come off.** They are left outside or just inside the entrance, and the host may offer slippers. Wherever there is a carpet, outdoor shoes don't go: people sit, eat and rest on the carpets of [A2 unit 4](a2-u04-culture).

**The best place goes to the guest.** In the felt tent this was the *tör*, the place of honour opposite the entrance, near the hearth. At family meals the eldest sat there, but when a guest came, the place was given to the guest as soon as he crossed the threshold, and the children stood up to greet him. In a modern flat the idea survives in the best seat, kept for the guest; and the same description says that the young sit down only when an elder invites them to.

**The meal is served on a cloth.** The *saçak* of [A1 unit 6](a1-u06-culture) is spread on the carpet or on a low table, and everyone sits around it. A cloth with food on it is treated with respect: it is not stepped on, and bread, which comes first, is never put on the floor or treated carelessly ([A1 unit 8](a1-u08-culture)). Break off a piece with your hands and taste it: refusing bread is rude. Green tea follows at once, poured into the bowl only part of the way and topped up again and again. You don't have to finish everything, but you will be offered more.

Visitors are usually given tea and food before anyone asks why they have come, and a quick visit can turn into a long meal. If you are invited, bring something small, such as sweets or a cake, and thank your hosts warmly when you leave.

blocks.title: Words for a visit
blocks.text: Your host will say *Hoş geldiňiz!* (welcome), *Içeri geçiň!* (come in), *Oturyň!* (sit down) and *Buýruň!* (please, help yourself). To refuse more, *Gerek däl, sag boluň*; and to promise another visit, *Ýene geleris!*
With this unit's `-mAlY`, you can read this:

blocks.tk: Şu gün biz Aýnalara barýarys. Gapyda aýakgaby çykarmaly. Myhman törde oturmaly. Ilki çörek we gök çaý gelýär. Çöregi ýere goýmaly däl. Biz hökman ýene geleris!
blocks.en: Today we're going to Aýna's family. At the door you have to take off your shoes. The guest should sit in the place of honour. First come bread and green tea. You mustn't put bread on the floor. We'll definitely come again!

vocab.en: the place of honour, opposite the door
the cloth spread for a meal

questions.q: Where does a guest traditionally sit?
options: in the place of honour, opposite the door
questions.explain: The *tör*, opposite the entrance: the best place goes to the guest.

questions.q: What should you do when you are offered bread?
options: break off a piece and taste it
put it on the floor beside you
questions.explain: Refusing bread is rude, and bread never goes on the floor.

questions.q: In the reading, what mustn't you do with bread?
questions.explain: *Çöregi ýere goýmaly däl*: you mustn't put bread on the floor.

sources.title: Traditions and customs of Turkmenistan
sources.note: A guest offered shelter and food in the first yurt; the saying “a guest comes, happiness comes”; the place of honour (tör) opposite the entrance, near the hearth, taken by the elder and given to a guest at the threshold; children standing to greet the guest

sources.title: Turkmen character and customs
sources.note: Shoes off wherever there is a carpet; tea and food before a visitor explains why he has come; a cloth with food on it is not stepped on; bread and salt held sacred; people judged by how they treat guests

sources.title: Dos and Don'ts in Central Asia
sources.note: Shoes off; the cloth spread on the floor or a low table, not to be stepped on; treat bread with respect, taste it, refusing is rude; tea half filled; no need to finish your plate; bring cake or sweets

sources.title: Traditional dwellings
sources.publisher: University of Washington, Silk Road Seattle
sources.note: In Central Asian yurts the seat of honour, tör, is opposite the entrance, for the elderly and guests
